I Created a Claude Skill for Processing Purchase Orders

A no-code solution for multi-document processing

Umair Ali Khan, Ph.D.
16 min read
·
Feb 5, 2026

If you are not a Medium member, you can read the full article at this link.

Picture this: It’s 4:47 PM on a Friday. Your customer just sent a Purchase Order (PO). Each product listed in the PO references a separate Bill of Materials (BoM), delivered as individual PDFs with detailed technical requirements. Your price list has hundreds of items.

You need to:

  1. Extract order details from the PO
  2. Match each line item (product) with its corresponding BoM
  3. Look up current prices for each product in the price table
  4. Calculate volume discounts and many other possible fees for each product
  5. Apply shipping, tax, and other rules
  6. Generate a sales order document following the company’s template
  7. Create an audit trail showing every calculation

You obviously need a significant amount of time to process this manually. Every field must be extracted correctly, and every calculation must be verified.

What if AI could do this in a minute?

What if you could just tell AI: “Process this purchase order,” and have it done?

That’s exactly what we are going to do in this article. We will build a Claude skill that transforms this process into a single command.

1. Introduction

A purchase order (PO) is a document issued by a buyer to a seller, outlining the types, specifications, quantities, and agreed-upon prices for products or services.

PO processing requires extracting structured information from the PO, such as item names, dimensions, quantities, and references. These fields then need to be matched against a master pricing spreadsheet to determine unit prices and a variety of fees, such as handling, cutting, testing, certification, and more.

These calculations often involve multiple decision points, such as volume discounts, delivery conditions, special packaging rules, and tax policies. While customers may include estimated prices in their purchase orders, those figures could be outdated or incorrect due to changes in supplier pricing or internal policies, or simple calculation errors. Therefore, suppliers must recalculate everything themselves.

In many cases, a purchase order may be split across multiple Bills of Material (BoMs), each containing detailed technical specifications for individual items. Processing such an order requires extracting line items from the PO, pulling corresponding material details from each BoM, locating the correct prices in a master price list, applying pricing rules and conditional logic, and finally generating a complete sales order with a clear price breakdown.

This process is time-consuming, manual, and error-prone. At the same time, it is highly repetitive, which makes it an excellent candidate for automation.

Yet applying AI here is not trivial. The workflow requires document parsing, reliable information extraction across multiple files, multi-step calculations, and the ability to merge all results into a final, auditable sales order.

This is where Claude Skills can help.

Claude Skills allow you to define repeatable workflows using instructions, reference documents, and guardrails that Claude can load dynamically. Instead of prompting ad hoc, you teach Claude how to perform a task consistently, ranging from extraction to calculation to output generation

In my previous articles, I have demonstrated how Claude Skills can be used effectively to automate repetitive workflows.

In this article, we will build a Claude skill that processes purchase orders and generates sales orders with accurate pricing. You can simply point Claude to a folder containing your PO, BoMs, and price list, and it will process the whole workflow as mentioned above.

The skill built in this article is use-case agnostic and can be easily adapted for other use cases (no programming required).

The skill-related resources are available in our GAIK project’s GitHub repository. In the same repository, you can also find other Claude skills (see the link), including report writing, voice-based incident reporting, and voice-driven construction site daily diary creation.

The repository link includes detailed guidelines for setting up and using the skill, along with sample data.

Note: For guidance on processing enterprise data securely, please refer to the recommendations in the last section.

Let’s dive in.

2. The Vision

The goal is to automate purchase order processing in a way that works regardless of how the information is structured.

We will focus on a more complex example in which a purchase order has multiple line items, where each item is linked to its own BoM. While the exact fields, pricing rules, and calculation logic may differ across industries and companies, the core automation idea remains the same.

The automated workflow is expected to follow a fixed sequence of steps every time.

Step 1: Collect the input documents

The workflow starts by gathering all required and optional inputs:

  • Purchase Order (required)
  • Bills of Material (BoMs) (if present)
  • Master price list (required)
  • Sample sales order (optional, used only for formatting reference)

Step 2: Extract structured data

The workflow then extracts the relevant fields from each document type. From the PO, this typically includes order number, customer details, line items and quantities, payment terms, and delivery information, etc.

From each BoM, it should extract fields such as material type and identifiers, dimensions and grades, technical specifications, and fee-related requirements (e.g., cutting, testing, certification, etc.), among others.

Step 3: Link PO items to BoMs

Each PO line item is then matched to its corresponding BoM. This is done by aligning a material number or other unique identifier and resolving which BoM belongs to which line item. Once linked, the PO item and its BoM are treated as a single logical unit for pricing.

Step 4: Retrieve pricing information

Using the material type and attributes extracted from the BoM, the workflow searches the master price list for exact matches and retrieves all relevant pricing components, for instance, unit price, cutting fees, testing fees, and certification fees, to name a few.

Step 5: Perform deterministic calculations

This includes line-item calculations, order-level aggregation, discounts, fees, shipping, taxes, and rounding rules. The calculation follows a fixed, transparent sequence with explicit decision points.

Here is an example calculation to give you an idea about the steps and decision points involved in a typical calculation. In Section 6, we will walk through a complete example using the same calculation logic to show how each step plays out in practice.

================================================================================
                        LINE ITEM CALCULATIONS
                     (Execute for EACH line item)
================================================================================

// Step 1: Material Cost
Material_Cost = Quantity × Unit_Price

// Step 2: Cutting Cost
Cutting_Cost = Cutting_Fee × Cuts_Per_Item
// Default: Cuts_Per_Item = 0 (if not specified in BoM)

// Step 3: Testing Cost
Testing_Cost = Testing_Fee × Lots_Per_Item
// Default: Lots_Per_Item = 1 (if not specified in BoM)

// Step 4: Certification Cost
Cert_Cost = Cert_Fee × Certs_Per_Item
// Default: Certs_Per_Item = 1 (if not specified in BoM)

// Step 5: Line Total
Line_Total = Material_Cost + Cutting_Cost + Testing_Cost + Cert_Cost


================================================================================
                        ORDER-LEVEL CALCULATIONS
================================================================================

// Step 6: Material Subtotal
Subtotal = Σ Material_Cost (for all items)

// Step 7: Determine Volume Discount Rate
IF Subtotal < $5,000:
    Discount_Rate = 0%
ELSE IF Subtotal < $15,000:
    Discount_Rate = 3%
ELSE IF Subtotal < $30,000:
    Discount_Rate = 5%
ELSE IF Subtotal < $50,000:
    Discount_Rate = 7%
ELSE:
    Discount_Rate = 10%

// Step 8: Calculate Volume Discount Amount
Volume_Discount = Subtotal × Discount_Rate

// Step 9: Net Material Cost (after discount)
Net_Material_Cost = Subtotal - Volume_Discount

// Step 10: Aggregate Cutting Fees
Total_Cutting_Fees = Σ Cutting_Cost (for all items)

// Step 11: Aggregate Testing Fees
Total_Testing_Fees = Σ Testing_Cost (for all items)

// Step 12: Aggregate Certification Fees
Total_Cert_Fees = Σ Cert_Cost (for all items)

// Step 13: Combined Total Fees
Total_Fees = Total_Cutting_Fees + Total_Testing_Fees + Total_Cert_Fees

// Step 14: Shipping (use PO value by default)
Shipping = PO_Shipping
// Alternative: Shipping = Total_Weight × Rate_Per_KG
// Alternative: Shipping = Flat_Rate (based on order size tier)

// Step 15: Taxable Amount (materials + fees + shipping)
Taxable_Amount = Net_Material_Cost + Total_Fees + Shipping

// Step 16: Tax Amount
Tax_Amount = Taxable_Amount × Tax_Rate
// Default: Tax_Rate = 6% (or from PO if specified)

// Step 17: Grand Total
Grand_Total = Net_Material_Cost + Total_Fees + Shipping + Tax_Amount

Step 6: Generate two documents:

  1. A professional sales order following the company’s template
  2. Complete audit trail showing the price calculation with every step

3. Creating the Claude Skill Package

A Claude skill is a package of one or more markdown files that guide Claude through multi-step workflows. For creating the PO processing workflow, we use the following skill architecture:

purchase-order-processing/
├── SKILL.md                              # Main orchestration file (required)
├── EVALUATION.md                         # Test scenarios and validation
└── reference/                            # Supporting specification files
    ├── EXTRACTION_FIELDS.md              # Field definitions and mappings
    ├── PRICING_RULES.md                  # Pricing logic and discount tiers
    ├── CALCULATION_LOGIC.md              # Calculation formulas
    ├── OUTPUT_FORMAT.md                  # Output specifications
    └── CALCULATION_BREAKDOWN_TEMPLATE.md # Audit trail format

The SKILL.md file (required) acts as the brain of the skill, defining when the skill should be activated, what inputs it expects, the step-by-step workflow Claude should follow, where detailed specifications (reference resources) are located, and the guardrails and error-handling rules.

While it is possible to define the entire skill in a single SKILL.md file, splitting the logic into multiple reference files leads to a smoother workflow and better readability.

Here is a minimal skeleton SKILL.md which highlights the main structural parts. The complete SKILL.md can be viewed in the GitHub repository.

# Skill Purpose
Converts a customer Purchase Order and related BoM documents into a priced Sales Order
using predefined pricing rules and deterministic calculations.

# Activation Conditions
Activate when a folder contains a Purchase Order document and a valid price list,
with optional BoM files for material breakdown.

# Input Documents
Defines the expected input structure:
– Purchase Order (PO)
– One or more BoM documents (optional)
– Master price list
– Optional sample Sales Order for formatting reference

# Data Extraction Scope
Specifies the fields to be extracted from the PO and BoMs, including customer details,
line items, quantities, materials, and project references.

# PO–BoM Matching Logic
Describes how PO line items are linked to BoM materials and how quantities are resolved
across documents.

# Pricing and Calculation Rules
References the pricing model, unit prices, fees, discounts, and calculation formulas
used to compute material costs and totals.

# Sales Order Generation
Defines how the final Sales Order is rendered, including structure, formatting rules,
and inclusion of a calculation breakdown.

# Error Handling and Guardrails
Rules for handling missing, ambiguous, or conflicting data and preventing hallucinated
values or calculations.

# Output Validation
Checks to ensure numerical correctness, pricing consistency, and compliance with the
expected Sales Order format.

# References and Specifications
Links to detailed reference files comprising extraction rules, pricing rules, 
calculation logic, output format, cost breakdown, and evaluation strategy.

The PO processing workflow is orchestrated by SKILL.md, which serves as the central control file for the skill. It references other markdown resources in the skill package that define how fields are extracted from the PO and BoMs, how pricing rules and calculation formulas are applied, how the output is formatted, and how the calculation breakdown is generated.

The following diagram shows the skill workflow.

4. How the Workflow Works

The workflow starts when customer documents are provided as input, including the PO, one or more BoMs (optionally), and a price list. These inputs are passed to SKILL.md, which acts as the main orchestrator and governs the entire execution flow.

First, SKILL.md validates the presence and structure of inputs and determines whether the skill should activate. Once activated, it initiates the data extraction phase by referring to EXTRACTION_FIELDS.md. This file defines which fields must be extracted from the PO and BoMs.

After extraction, SKILL.md coordinates the pricing and computation phase. It references PRICING_RULES.md to identify applicable unit prices, fees, discounts, and pricing constraints, and then applies CALCULATION_LOGIC.md to perform cost calculations.

Once pricing and calculations are complete, SKILL.md moves to output generation. It uses OUTPUT_FORMAT.md to control the structure and layout of the final sales order and CALCULATION_BREAKDOWN_TEMPLATE.md to generate a transparent, itemized explanation of how each cost and total was derived.

Before finalizing the output, the workflow is validated against EVALUATION.md. This file defines test scenarios and validation criteria that are used to check numerical correctness, rule compliance, and structural consistency of the generated sales order and calculation breakdown.

Once all validations pass, the skill produces the output, consisting of a formatted sales order accompanied by a detailed calculation breakdown.

5. Deploying the Skill Package

Install Claude Desktop, which provides a persistent execution environment and full Skills support similar to the web version, but with better local testing, file handling, and integration continuity. Desktop makes Skills feel more like a native app with full control over uploaded resources.

To enable Claude Desktop to use the local filesystem for Skills, you must configure its MCP servers. This allows Claude to access files on your machine when processing tasks like PO/BoM processing.

Open the Claude Desktop app and sign in with your account. Open the Claude Desktop config file. Press Win + R, and enter:

%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json

Press Enter. Add or update the mcpServers section so it includes the filesystem server:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "filesystem": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "C:\\"]
    }
  }
}

Save and close the file. Quit Claude Desktop completely (including the system tray), and launch it again.

You should now see the filesystem MCP server as one of the connectors:

Zip the entire skill folder (purchase-order-processing) and make sure it has the same structure as shown above. This zip will become the upload package.

In Claude Desktop, go to Settings → Capabilities and make sure that Code execution and file creation option is turned on. This is required so that Claude can load, analyze, and execute workflows defined by your skill file.

Still in Settings → Capabilities, scroll to the “Skills” section and click “+Add.” Select your zip file and upload it.

Once uploaded, Claude will register it and list it among available skills.

For testing skill, create a folder for the input documents with the following structure:

My-Order/
├── customer_data/           ← REQUIRED: Put PO and BoMs here
│   ├── PO.pdf
│   ├── BOM1.pdf
│   ├── BOM2.pdf
│   └── BOM3.pdf
├── price_list/              ← REQUIRED: Put your price list here
│   └── price_list.xlsx
└── sample_sales_order/      ← OPTIONAL: Put a sample SO format here
    └── sample_order.docx

You can have a purchase order without BoMs. The skill will detect the PO structure automatically.

In Claude Desktop, upload the .zip file of the documents (same structure) and type:

Process these documents using purchase-order-processing skill

Or provide the local path of the documents:

Generate a sales order from C:\Orders\NewCustomer using purchase-order-processing skill

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Material Subtotal: $25,567.50

DISCOUNT TIER DETERMINATION:
  From Price List - Volume Discount Schedule:
  - $0 - $4,999:        0%
  - $5,000 - $14,999:   3%
  - $15,000 - $29,999:  5%  ← APPLICABLE TIER
  - $30,000 - $49,999:  7%
  - $50,000+:          10%

  Applicable Discount Rate: 5%

CALCULATION:
  Discount Amount = Material Subtotal × Discount Rate
                  = $25,567.50 × 5%
                  = $25,567.50 × 0.05
                  = $1,278.375
                  = $1,278.38 (rounded to nearest cent)

                    = $25,567.50 - $1,278.38

7. Potential Extensions & Considerations

There are several ways this skill can be extended and refined.

One enhancement is the addition of reference scripts (for example, in Python) to accelerate specific parts of the workflow and make them more deterministic. These scripts could handle tasks such as PDF parsing, price lookup in Excel tables, price calculations, and generating the final sales order in .docx format.

Another useful extension could be a dedicated verification step. This step could recheck extracted fields and calculated prices to ensure accuracy and consistency before generating the final output.

Another concern from businesses could be exposing confidential customer documents to AI models. For this, use the Claude skill with Claude SDK agents via a secure environment, such as Microsoft Azure API endpoint for Claude models. This allows you to process documents without your data being used to train the models. Also, Claude for Enterprise/Team plans offer higher data privacy standards compared to the free consumer version.

Because the skill is written in natural language, it is easy to understand, modify, and adapt. This makes it straightforward for users to customize the workflow for their own use cases without changing the overall structure.

If you try this skill or adapt it for your own workflows, I would be interested to hear about your experience. If you run into issues or edge cases, feel free to share them in the comments.
